summaries.title: Distributed Representations Explained
summaries.gist: Distributed representations actually combine two distinct, competing strategies—composition and superposition—that trade off against each other and must be told apart to understand neural networks.
summaries.question: What do neural networks' "distributed representations" really consist of, and how do superposition and composition relate? (an argument)

summaries.title: Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition
summaries.gist: Distributed representations split into two ideas, composition and superposition, illustrated by four codes for colored shapes ranging from one-neuron-per-object to fully overlapping codes.
summaries.question: What are the different kinds of "distributed" codes for representing colored shapes, and what do they trade off? (four example codes)

summaries.title: Two notions of distributed representation
summaries.gist: The term "distributed representation" actually names two different ideas, composition and superposition, which trade off against each other and are illustrated using Thorpe's four example codes for colored shapes.

summaries.title: "Local" Codes
summaries.gist: A pure local code, with one neuron per shape-color pair and no superposition, wastes neurons but lets a later layer linearly select almost any combination of stimuli, unlike other codes.

summaries.title: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes
summaries.gist: Representing independent features like color and shape separately, then composing them, uses far fewer neurons, generalizes across combinations, and stays easy to interpret component by component.

summaries.title: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes
summaries.gist: A dense code can represent far more unrelated objects than it has neurons by packing color-shape pairs into superposition, but this sacrifices linear probing and requires abandoning composition entirely.

summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition are not points on one spectrum but opposite strategies for allocating the same exponential representational capacity, so gains from one come at the expense of the other.
summaries.question: Are composition and superposition just degrees of the same "distributed" spectrum, or opposing strategies? (a mathematical argument)

summaries.title: A false spectrum of distributedness
summaries.gist: The local, semi-local, and highly-distributed codes look like one continuous spectrum of increasing distributedness, but this framing hides that two different strategies are at work.

summaries.title: Volume allocation argument
summaries.gist: With m bits giving exponential volume, fully composable features need exponential storage themselves, so a representation can either compose features fully or store exponentially many items in superposition, not both.

summaries.title: Mixing Composition and Superposition
summaries.gist: Because real features are sparse and rarely co-occur, composition leaves unused regions of representational space that networks can exploit to store additional features in superposition.
summaries.question: Can composition and superposition coexist despite competing for the same capacity? (yes, via sparsity)

summaries.title: Sparsity enables mixing
summaries.gist: When feature combinations are sparse rather than dense, the compositional space contains low-probability "holes" that networks can fill by storing additional features in superposition.

summaries.title: Semi-distributed code example
summaries.gist: Thorpe's semi-distributed code composes color and shape features as before, but puts colors in mutual superposition and shapes in mutual superposition, best understood via neuron-combination directions.

summaries.title: Conclusion
summaries.gist: Distinguishing composition from superposition matters because they have very different properties, and understanding which one structures a network's representations is key to reverse-engineering it.
summaries.question: Why does it matter to separate composition from superposition in distributed representations? (a summary claim)

summaries.title: Two tensioned notions
summaries.gist: "Distributed representations" names two different things, superposition and composition, which can mix but remain fundamentally in tension and have very different properties worth distinguishing.

summaries.title: Why this matters for interpretability
summaries.gist: Composed representations can be understood using only a linear number of independent features rather than exponential volume, which is critical for truly understanding neural networks.

glossary.name: superposition
glossary.senseHere: A strategy where a network packs more features than it has neurons by storing them as overlapping directions in activation space, retrievable only with the help of a non-linearity; it lets a small number of neurons encode an exponentially large number of possible stimuli, but at the cost of losing the ability to cleanly read off any one feature with a simple linear probe.

glossary.name: distributed representation
glossary.senseHere: A representation where a stimulus is encoded by a pattern across several neurons rather than by one dedicated neuron. The piece argues this umbrella term actually hides two different, competing strategies - composition and superposition - that are often conflated despite having very different properties.

glossary.name: composition
glossary.senseHere: A strategy where independent features (like color and shape) are each given their own neuron and objects are represented by combining several such feature-neurons at once; this lets a linear number of neurons cover an exponential number of combinations, generalizes to unseen combinations, and stays interpretable feature-by-feature, but only works if the combinations don't need to be packed as densely as superposition allows.

glossary.name: Thorpe (1989)
glossary.background: A neuroscience paper by Simon Thorpe that used shape-and-color neuron examples to illustrate a spectrum from 'local' to 'distributed' neural codes, including local, semi-local, semi-distributed, and highly-distributed variants.

glossary.name: linear probe
glossary.senseHere: A simple linear function trained to detect whether a particular feature (like 'red') is present, applied to a layer's neuron activations. The piece uses it as a test of whether a feature is cleanly and reliably represented, noting that a probe can succeed even in a 'local code' where treating the result as a genuine feature would be misleading, while it generally fails on features hidden in dense superposition.

glossary.name: Toy Models of Superposition
glossary.senseHere: Referred to here as the authors' earlier paper exploring the same composition/superposition trade-off, but framed there in terms of 'feature sparsity' rather than composition.
